entry.description: A convex-body variant of Soberon's counterexample to the Grunbaum conjecture. The primary source reports: The source reports a construction of a convex body with nonempty interior in R^4 for which no four affine hyperplanes divide its uniform volume into sixteen equal sign cells. It reports an adaptation of Soberon's counterexample for a smooth positive density using a Wulff-body perturbation; it does not preserve the source's smooth-density property. Further checking: Ask Soberon/independent discrete geometers to review the Wulff perturbation and novelty of the uniform-convex-body strengthening; replay the Lean development; check the arbitrary-normal bridge; and retain the distinction from the smooth-density theorem. entry.description: Hausdorff-dimension and positive-measure bounds for (n,k)-Besicovitch sets. The primary source reports: Let p_c be the root in (2,3) of p^3-2p^2-2p+2=0. The source reports Hausdorff dimension at least n-(n-k)/p_c^k for every (n,k)-Besicovitch set with 1<=k<=n, and positive Lebesgue measure for measurable such sets when p_c^(k-1)+k>n. It claims to transfer the Katz-Tao numerical exponent to Hausdorff dimension and improve Oberlin's displayed range; it does not claim the best bound in every dimension or the full conjecture. entry.description: Sharp cup powers and size bounds for locally profinite spaces. entry.description: The large sieve for square moduli under Hooley's hypothesis $R^*$. The primary source reports: The paper reports that conditionally improves the relevant large-sieve exponent for square moduli from 1/2 to 1/2-1/134 at N=Q^3 under Hooley's hypothesis R*. The primary source directly reports this AI involvement: The work proceeded in rounds. Claude produced a complete draft; the author examined it against his own understanding of the problem and returned lists of objections, requests for detail, and questions – about which steps were justified, which characters were actually being summed over, whether a bound really was uniform in the modulus, where an error term would arise and how large it would be – and Claude answered each either with a proof or with a correction. entry.description: Benign Nonconvex Landscape for Policy Optimization: Infinite-Horizon Discounted MDPs with General State and Action Spaces. The primary source reports: The paper reports that gives weaker conditions ensuring no suboptimal stationary points and a PLK inequality for policy optimization, with convergence rates. The primary source directly reports this AI involvement: Reinforcement learning (RL) has found applications in a wide range of domains, including game-playing AI (Mnih et al. 2015, Silver et al. 2016), the training of large language models (Ouyang et al. 2022, Guo et al. 2025), robotics (Kober et al. 2013, Hwangbo et al. 2019), healthcare (Komorowski et al. 2018), and operations management (Gijsbrechts et al. 2022, Alvo et al. 2023). Policy gradient methods constitute an important class of RL algorithms that directly optimize a parameterized policy by applying first-order methods to its expected cumulative cost (Sutton et al. 1999, Silver et al. 2014). This approach is particularly attractive for Markov Decision Processes (MDPs) with continuous state and action spaces, where solving the Bellman equation over all admissible policies can be difficult, while structural analysis often identifies a low-dimensional policy class containing an optimal policy. Classic examples include linear policies for linear quadratic regulator (LQR) problems and base-stock policies for inventory models. Parameterizing such a policy class reduces the original control problem to a finite-dimensional optimization problem. However, the resulting objective is generally nonconvex (Agarwal et al. 2021), so first-order stationarity alone does not guarantee global optimality. contribution.rationale: Reinforcement learning (RL) has found applications in a wide range of domains, including game-playing AI (Mnih et al. 2015, Silver et al. 2016), the training of large language models (Ouyang et al. 2022, Guo et al. 2025), robotics (Kober et al. 2013, Hwangbo et al. 2019), healthcare (Komorowski et al. 2018), and operations management (Gijsbrechts et al. 2022, Alvo et al. 2023). Policy gradient methods constitute an important class of RL algorithms that directly optimize a parameterized policy by applying first-order methods to its expected cumulative cost (Sutton et al. 1999, Silver et al. 2014). This approach is particularly attractive for Markov Decision Processes (MDPs) with continuous state and action spaces, where solving the Bellman equation over all admissible policies can be difficult, while structural analysis often identifies a low-dimensional policy class containing an optimal policy. Classic examples include linear policies for linear quadratic regulator (LQR) problems and base-stock policies for inventory models. Parameterizing such a policy class reduces the original control problem to a finite-dimensional optimization problem. However, the resulting objective is generally nonconvex (Agarwal et al. 2021), so first-order stationarity alone does not guarantee global optimality.
